paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove a data point's influence from a trained model without paying the full cost of retraining. A complication arises when deletion requests depend on models already released. Someone might request deletion after seeing what a model reveals about them, so the model and the sequence of requests become connected.

This paper addresses that adaptive setting. It develops a general reduction that lets guarantees for deletion sequences chosen independently of published models support guarantees for adaptive sequences. The reduction uses differential privacy and its connection to max information to manage the dependence introduced by observing model outputs.

Combined with existing approaches for non-adaptive deletion, the result supports flexible algorithms with provable adaptive deletion guarantees across arbitrary model classes and training methods. The authors also show theoretically why earlier non-convex approaches can fail under adaptive requests. They turn that reasoning into a practical attack on SISA using CIFAR-10, MNIST, and Fashion-MNIST, demonstrating why the distinction between adaptive and non-adaptive requests matters.
neurips-2021-adaptive-machine-unlearning.tldr: The paper uses differential privacy to extend machine-unlearning guarantees to deletion requests that depend on previously published models.

paragraphs: Generating a medical report from an image usually requires training examples that pair each image with its corresponding report. Collecting those matched examples is expensive and time-consuming. This paper proposes Knowledge Graph Auto-Encoder, or KGAE, which can instead train on separate collections of medical images and reports.

The central device is a preconstructed knowledge graph that supplies a shared representation for visual and textual information. A knowledge-driven encoder maps an image or report to coordinates in that shared space. A knowledge-driven decoder then turns a coordinate into report text. This common space provides the bridge that paired examples would otherwise help establish.

The experiments report desirable generated reports without any image-report training pairs. KGAE also accepts paired data, allowing the same framework to operate in semi-supervised and supervised settings. After additional fine-tuning on matched images and reports, it consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art models on two datasets. The findings therefore support both learning without pairs and using pairs to improve an already trained system.
neurips-2021-auto-encoding-knowledge-gra.tldr: KGAE uses a shared knowledge-graph representation to learn medical report generation from separate image and report collections.

paragraphs: A delusive attack changes the features of training examples slightly while leaving their labels correct. Its goal is to make a learner perform poorly on ordinary test data. Because the labels remain intact, the damage comes from what the altered examples encourage the model to learn.

The paper formalizes the attacker as choosing worst-case training data within a particular infinity-Wasserstein ball, which constrains the permitted changes. Within this formulation, minimizing adversarial risk on the corrupted data is equivalent to optimizing an upper bound on ordinary risk for the original data. This relationship supplies a theoretical reason to use adversarial training as a defense.

The authors also examine how the defense works. In a natural setting, adversarial training can prevent excessive dependence on non-robust features that delusive perturbations exploit. Experiments on benchmark datasets show the defense withstanding six practical attacks and largely recovering the test accuracy lost to corruption. These findings support adversarial training for the studied threat, with the theoretical justification tied to the specified attack formulation.
neurips-2021-better-safe-than-sorry-prev.tldr: Adversarial training offers a theoretically motivated defense against small training-data perturbations designed to damage ordinary test accuracy.

paragraphs: Graph embeddings turn relationships into representations that learning systems can optimize. Although Euclidean vectors can theoretically represent any graph, other geometries may fit particular graph structures more naturally. The paper examines why such alternatives often help at small representation sizes but lose their advantage as the number of dimensions increases.

The authors introduce a box-embedding variant with a learned smoothing parameter. It provides greater representational capacity than vector models in low dimensions while avoiding the performance saturation observed in other geometric models at higher dimensions. They also prove that box embeddings can represent any directed acyclic graph, establishing a broad expressiveness result for graphs without directed cycles.

The empirical study compares vector, hyperbolic, and region-based representations on several families of synthetic and real directed graphs. It identifies correlations among graph characteristics, graph family, model size, and embedding geometry. These results help explain the structural preferences built into different representations: choosing a geometry affects which relationships are convenient to learn, even when multiple representations have substantial theoretical capacity.
neurips-2021-capacity-and-bias-of-learne.tldr: A box-embedding model with learned smoothing improves capacity across dimensions, while theory and experiments clarify how geometry fits directed graphs.

paragraphs: A text classifier may rely on details that an analyst considers irrelevant to its task. For example, changing a subject's gender might change a sentiment prediction. Stress tests expose this behavior by modifying irrelevant information and checking whether the prediction moves with it.

This paper uses causal inference to formalize the desired stability as counterfactual invariance. It connects that property to performance outside the training domain and develops practical methods for learning approximately invariant predictors without requiring counterfactual examples. This makes the formal requirement relevant even when training data do not contain matched examples of the changes one wants a model to ignore.

The crucial finding is that the appropriate learning method depends on how the data are causally generated. In particular, a setting where labels cause features differs from one where features cause labels. These structures require different regularization schemes and support different domain-shift guarantees. Text-classification experiments support the theory, showing why a single recipe for removing spurious dependence cannot be assumed to carry the same implications across causal settings.
neurips-2021-counterfactual-invariance-t.tldr: The paper formalizes prediction stability under irrelevant changes and shows that achieving it and benefiting from it depend on causal structure.

paragraphs: A molecular representation determines which information a learning system can use when predicting molecular properties. PhysChem builds that representation by combining physical and chemical information. Its architecture gives these two sources of information specialized networks that cooperate rather than asking one undifferentiated component to learn everything.

The physical component, PhysNet, learns molecular conformations by simulating molecular dynamics with parameterized forces. The chemical component, ChemNet, uses geometry-aware message passing to learn chemical and biomedical properties. This means its exchange of information takes molecular geometry into account. The networks retain their separate tasks while supplying useful information to each other.

That cooperation is the paper's central contribution: learning physical structure and learning molecular properties become connected parts of representation learning. The authors report state-of-the-art performance on MoleculeNet and further evidence of effectiveness on SARS-CoV-2 datasets. These empirical findings support the proposed combination of physical and chemical information for the evaluated molecular learning tasks, rather than assessing the two components only as isolated predictors.
neurips-2021-deep-molecular-representati.tldr: PhysChem combines a neural molecular-dynamics component with geometry-aware chemical learning to improve molecular representations and property prediction.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent estimates a full-data gradient from a small minibatch. Uniform sampling is common, but the resulting estimate can be noisy. Determinantal point processes, or DPPs, favor diverse selections, making them a candidate for obtaining more informative minibatches. This paper develops a principled account of when that diversity helps.

The method constructs DPPs using orthogonal polynomials and information about the data distribution. Its analysis connects the finite dataset with an underlying continuous domain. For specific DPPs and controlled approximations, the authors show that gradient-estimator variance can decrease faster as batch size grows than it does with uniform sampling.

Combined with existing finite-time results for convex objectives, this yields a smaller mean-square approximation-error bound when batches are sufficiently large and the total budget of individual gradient evaluations is fixed. The estimators also work with an algorithm that samples the required aggregate directly, without first sampling a minibatch, reducing overhead. Synthetic and real-data experiments support the theoretical claims. The advantage is therefore conditional on the analyzed constructions and optimization setting.
neurips-2021-determinantal-point-process.tldr: Distribution-aware DPP minibatches can reduce gradient variance faster than uniform sampling and improve convex-SGD error bounds under stated conditions.

paragraphs: Diffusion normalizing flow generates data by learning a relationship between the data distribution and Gaussian noise. It uses two neural stochastic differential equations, which describe transformations that include randomness. One gradually adds noise to data; the other gradually removes noise to produce samples.

The two directions are trained jointly using a shared cost that measures their difference. Through this training, the backward process converges to a diffusion that begins with a Gaussian distribution and ends with the desired data distribution. The forward transformation and the generative transformation are therefore learned together as parts of one objective.

The approach combines ideas from normalizing flows and diffusion probabilistic models. The authors report that it can learn distributions with sharp boundaries, an advantage over normalizing flow, and requires fewer discretization steps than diffusion probabilistic models, improving sampling efficiency. It also achieves competitive results in high-dimensional density estimation and image generation. These findings connect the method's distribution-modeling capabilities with the computational work needed to draw samples.
neurips-2021-diffusion-normalizing-flow-.tldr: Diffusion normalizing flow jointly learns noise-adding and noise-removing stochastic processes to combine flexible density modeling with more efficient sampling.

paragraphs: EditGAN lets users modify an image by editing detailed masks that identify its parts. A user might redraw a car's headlight region to request a corresponding image change. This provides fine control over meaningful components, addressing the coarse controls and extensive annotation requirements of many earlier GAN editing methods.

The underlying GAN models images and their semantic segmentations together and needs only a handful of labeled examples. To perform an edit, the system embeds an image in the GAN's latent space, then optimizes that representation to satisfy the changed segmentation. Altering the representation also changes the generated image.

To avoid repeating the full optimization for every use, EditGAN learns reusable editing vectors that can be applied to other images at interactive rates. The experiments show detailed edits that preserve image quality, combinations of multiple edits, and plausible modifications beyond the training data. Evaluations across varied image types also outperform several earlier methods on standard editing benchmarks. The reusable vectors connect precise optimization-based editing with faster subsequent interaction.
neurips-2021-editgan-high-precision-sema.tldr: EditGAN turns detailed segmentation-mask changes into image edits and learns reusable latent-space vectors for interactive editing.

paragraphs: Success in competitive games does not directly answer whether an AI makes a good human teammate. This study investigates that question in Hanabi, a cooperative card game. It compares human teams playing with a rule-based agent, SmartBot, and a learning-based agent, Other-Play, using a single-blind evaluation.

The evaluation measures both game score and the human experience of collaboration. Participants assess perceived performance, teamwork, interpretability, trust, and overall teammate preference. Measuring these separately allows the study to examine whether similar task outcomes can coexist with different judgments about how understandable or desirable a teammate is.

Participants clearly preferred SmartBot across nearly all subjective measures and generally judged Other-Play negatively. Yet the game scores showed no statistically significant difference. That result does not establish that the agents have identical performance; it shows that the measured subjective preference was not accompanied by a statistically detected score difference. The study argues that AI teammate design and reinforcement-learning benchmarks should include human assessments alongside objective performance, because scores alone missed an important distinction in this evaluation.
neurips-2021-evaluation-of-human-ai-team.tldr: Human Hanabi players preferred a rule-based AI teammate over a learning-based one despite no statistically significant difference in game score.

paragraphs: A neural network's starting parameter scales can make training unstable or complicate the choice of optimization settings. Initialization rules designed for one architecture may not transfer well to another. GradInit addresses this with an automated initialization method intended to work across architectures.

Its guiding idea is to choose parameter scales that make a single optimizer step effective. With SGD or Adam settings prescribed, GradInit adjusts each layer's norm to minimize the loss after that step. It introduces a scalar multiplier for each parameter block and optimizes those multipliers numerically, making the initial scales responsive to the intended training procedure.

The reported results show faster convergence and improved test performance across several convolutional architectures, including networks with and without skip connections and networks without normalization layers. GradInit also stabilizes the original Transformer for machine translation. In that setting, it enables training without learning-rate warmup using either Adam or SGD across a wide range of learning rates and momentum values. These results support initialization based on anticipated optimization behavior rather than architecture-specific rules alone.
neurips-2021-gradinit-learning-to-initia.tldr: GradInit learns parameter-block scales that make an initial optimizer step effective, improving training stability and convergence across tested architectures.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers useful information from a teacher model to a student. For object detection, deciding what to transfer is complicated because different image locations contribute differently to identifying and locating each object. A uniform treatment of the teacher's representations can therefore be difficult to balance.

This paper conditions distillation on each target instance. A learnable decoding module encodes information about the instance as an attention query and uses teacher representations as keys. The resulting attention measures which features contribute to that instance. An auxiliary task sensitive to both recognition and localization guides this selection, aligning the transferred information with both parts of detection.

Experiments show improvements across multiple settings. In one reported result, RetinaNet with a ResNet-50 backbone improves from 37.4 to 40.7 mAP under a 1× training schedule. That score exceeds the teacher's 40.4 mAP with a ResNet-101 backbone under a 3× schedule. This demonstrates that instance-conditioned transfer can improve a student substantially and, in the reported configuration, even surpass its teacher.
neurips-2021-instance-conditional-knowle.tldr: Instance-conditioned attention selects teacher features useful for recognizing and locating each object, improving detector distillation.

paragraphs: Question-answering models can exploit dataset shortcuts, such as language priors in visual questions or answer-position patterns in reading comprehension. Debiasing can improve performance when those patterns change, but existing approaches may lose substantial accuracy when test examples follow the original training distribution.

Introspective Distillation, or IntroD, aims to balance those two needs. For each training sample, it assesses whether the example fits the factual, in-distribution setting or a counterfactual, out-of-distribution setting. It then blends the inductive biases associated with those settings. The central idea is to make this blend sensitive to the sample rather than imposing the same preference throughout training.

The authors evaluate IntroD on the visual question-answering datasets VQA v2 and VQA-CP and the reading-comprehension dataset SQuAD. They report competitive out-of-distribution performance relative to other debiasing approaches, together with little loss or even improvement in in-distribution performance relative to methods without debiasing. These findings indicate that the observed tradeoff can be reduced in the evaluated tasks, supporting robustness without routinely surrendering performance on familiar data.
neurips-2021-introspective-distillation-.tldr: IntroD adapts the blend of in-distribution and out-of-distribution learning biases to improve question-answering robustness while preserving familiar-distribution performance.

paragraphs: An AI can play a multiplayer online battle arena game extremely well while still using a limited range of strategies. This paper treats strategic diversity as a distinct learning objective. Its Macro-Goals Guided framework, MGG, uses high-level goals to encourage different policies rather than relying on strong game performance alone to produce variety.

MGG extracts macro-goals from human demonstrations and trains a Meta-Controller to predict them. During training, it samples goals from the Meta-Controller's predictions and guides learning toward the selected goals. Human demonstrations thus supply strategic abstractions, while sampling creates opportunities to train behavior directed at different strategies.

Experiments in Honor of Kings show that MGG executes diverse policies across matches and team lineups. The authors also report outperforming state-of-the-art methods over 102 heroes. These results matter because the framework pursues variation in play while also delivering strong measured performance. The evidence supports macro-goal guidance as a way to broaden the policies learned in the evaluated game, rather than treating diversity as an automatic consequence of competitive strength.
neurips-2021-learning-diverse-policies-i.tldr: MGG samples high-level goals learned from human demonstrations to train diverse, strong policies in Honor of Kings.

paragraphs: NANSY is a speech analysis and synthesis framework for controlling voice, pitch, and speaking speed. Earlier approaches often separate controllable attributes by restricting information through a bottleneck, which can harm reconstruction quality. This paper instead changes the information presented during training.

The training strategy perturbs properties of the original signal, including formants, pitch, and frequency response. These perturbations encourage synthesis networks to selectively use the attributes needed to reconstruct the input. Without requiring a bottleneck structure, NANSY can retain high reconstruction quality while supporting control over speech attributes.

The system uses wav2vec features and a proposed pitch representation called Yingram, allowing fully self-supervised training without text or speaker labels. Training on a multilingual dataset also extends the framework to multiple languages. Experiments report significant improvements in applications including zero-shot voice conversion, pitch shifting, and time-scale modification. Together, the results support information perturbation as a way to learn controllable speech synthesis while avoiding the reconstruction tradeoff associated with the bottleneck approaches discussed in the paper.
neurips-2021-neural-analysis-and-synthes.tldr: NANSY uses information perturbations and self-supervised speech features to support high-quality reconstruction with control over voice, pitch, and speed.

paragraphs: Movement control must cope with sensory information that is both noisy and delayed. Optimal feedback control addresses this by combining observations with an internal model's predictions and choosing actions that optimize relevant behavioral criteria. Translating that framework into a plausible neural learning mechanism has remained challenging.

The paper combines adaptive Kalman filtering with a model-free policy-gradient controller in an online algorithm. A neural implementation uses local synaptic plasticity rules to learn system properties, estimate state, and control behavior. Its internal model helps estimate the current state despite delayed sensory feedback.

The approach learns system identification and filtering without separate training phases or prior knowledge of noise covariances. Its controller also learns without requiring known system dynamics, avoiding the need for weight transport. This brings estimation and action learning together rather than considering filtering alone. The contribution is a biologically plausible implementation that addresses the credit-assignment problem for the studied delayed, noisy control setting: local updates support learning the computations needed to produce appropriate movements.
neurips-2021-neural-optimal-feedback-con.tldr: An online neural controller combines adaptive state estimation and policy-gradient learning using local plasticity rules to handle noisy, delayed feedback.

paragraphs: Prediction systems often benefit from structural assumptions that match the task. Symmetries are one source of such assumptions, but discovering useful ones automatically is difficult. This paper focuses on sequential prediction and asks whether a model can learn quantities whose conservation helps it predict.

Inspired by Noether's theorem, the authors formulate the search for useful inductive biases as meta-learning conserved quantities. Their Noether Network architecture includes a learned conservation loss that is optimized inside the prediction function. Consequently, conservation is an active part of producing a prediction, rather than merely an observation made after training.

The authors provide theoretical and experimental evidence that this architecture improves prediction quality. The significance is the route to finding structure: the system learns which conservation-based constraint is useful instead of relying entirely on a manually selected symmetry. The paper presents this as a general framework for discovering inductive biases in sequential problems. Its findings support the usefulness of learned conservation objectives without implying that every sequence must follow a particular predefined physical conservation law.
neurips-2021-noether-networks-meta-learn.tldr: Noether Networks meta-learn conservation objectives and optimize them during prediction to discover useful structure in sequential tasks.

paragraphs: A neuron's computation depends on both its incoming connections and its intrinsic properties. Connections determine which inputs arrive, while cellular parameters shape how those inputs unfold over time. This paper extends learning beyond synaptic weights to include intrinsic parameters such as time constants and reset potential.

The learning process uses sparse feedback specifying target spike times and gradient-based updates to both kinds of parameters. In a teacher-student setup, a randomly initialized leaky integrate-and-fire or resonate-and-fire neuron attempts to recover a teacher neuron's parameters. This provides a concrete test of learning the temporal behavior of a neuron rather than adjusting connectivity alone.

The results show that complex temporal input-output functions can be learned online using event-based updates, without backpropagation through time. The contribution connects learnable intrinsic dynamics with a sparse feedback mechanism that is biologically inspired. The authors describe it as a step toward learning neural computations from feedback that supplies neither a graded score nor a signed correction, emphasizing the potential of timing information to guide adaptation.
neurips-2021-online-learning-of-neural-c.tldr: Sparse target-spike feedback can train both synaptic weights and intrinsic neuron parameters online without backpropagation through time.

paragraphs: In reinforcement learning, the representation of state-action values can affect how much performance an agent loses while learning. This paper studies finite-horizon Markov decision processes with linear structure and asks when regret can remain bounded by a constant, rather than continuing to increase as learning proceeds.

The authors derive a necessary representation condition called universally spanning optimal features, or UNISOFT, for constant regret in any MDP with a linear reward function. They then establish sufficiency for low-rank MDPs and the more general class with zero inherent Bellman error. For these classes, they prove constant-regret bounds for the optimistic algorithms LSVI-UCB and ELEANOR.

The paper also develops an algorithm that selects among supplied representations. It achieves constant regret when one representation, or a suitable combination of them, satisfies UNISOFT. The result links learning efficiency to a precise property of the available features. Its guarantee is conditional: representation selection delivers the stated bound when the candidate collection contains the required structure, either directly or through combination.
neurips-2021-reinforcement-learning-in-l.tldr: The paper characterizes representation conditions for constant regret in linear MDPs and proves a conditional guarantee for selecting suitable representations.

paragraphs: Channel pruning compresses a convolutional network by removing filters judged redundant. Many criteria assign each filter an importance score, but this paper asks whether those scores actually lead to meaningfully different or informative decisions. Its experiments identify two weaknesses in widely used criteria.

First, several prominent criteria produce almost the same filter ranking, so comparing their formulas can overstate how different their pruning behavior is. Second, some criteria assign scores that are too similar to distinguish redundancy clearly. The authors analyze these issues for both layer-wise pruning and global pruning, where the scope of the selection differs.

The analysis also challenges the assumption that pruning based on the ℓ1 and ℓ2 norms always produces similar results. Its reasoning combines empirical experiments with an assumption that well-trained filters within a layer have an approximately Gaussian-like distribution, supported by extensive statistical tests. The findings encourage judging a criterion by its actual rankings and ability to separate filters, while retaining the distributional assumption underlying the analysis.
neurips-2021-rethinking-the-pruning-crit.tldr: The paper shows that common CNN pruning criteria can produce nearly identical rankings or poorly separated scores, complicating claims about filter importance.

paragraphs: Contrastive self-supervised learning has produced useful visual representations, but much of its use has centered on curated datasets. This paper investigates how dataset composition affects those methods. It finds that MoCo works well across object-focused and scene-focused data, balanced and long-tailed distributions, and general and domain-specific collections.

Building on that observed flexibility, the authors examine modest changes to the learning procedure. Multi-scale cropping, stronger augmentations, and nearest neighbors introduce additional invariances and improve the learned representations. The study therefore connects broader applicability with adjustments to what the model is encouraged to treat as equivalent.

A further finding concerns spatial information. With a multi-crop training strategy, MoCo learns representations that retain useful spatial structure. Those representations support semantic segment retrieval and video instance segmentation without fine-tuning, with results comparable to specialized models. This shows that the learned features can support region-level uses as well as broader image representation tasks, under the evaluated training strategy and applications.
neurips-2021-revisiting-contrastive-meth.tldr: MoCo works across varied dataset types, and simple training changes improve representations while enabling spatial tasks without fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning often compares transformed views of the same observation, with the expectation that transformations preserve meaningful content. This paper gives that intuition a latent-variable formulation. It divides the hidden representation into content assumed unchanged by augmentation and style allowed to vary.

The analysis permits substantial statistical and causal dependencies among latent variables. It establishes sufficient conditions under which paired views identify the invariant content component in both generative and discriminative settings. Identification is up to an invertible mapping: the content can be recovered in a transformed representation without requiring its original coordinates.

Numerical simulations with dependent latent variables agree with the theory. The authors also introduce Causal3DIdent, a dataset of visually complex, high-dimensional images with rich causal dependencies, to examine practical augmentation choices. The contribution explains when augmentation-based learning can isolate content even without independent hidden factors. Its guarantees depend on the stated content-invariance model and sufficient conditions, so the results do not imply that arbitrary augmentations always recover the intended semantics.
neurips-2021-self-supervised-learning-wi.tldr: Under sufficient conditions, paired augmented views identify invariant content up to an invertible mapping even when latent factors have causal and statistical dependencies.

paragraphs: This paper treats trained neural networks themselves as the objects to represent. Rather than learning features of images or text, it learns features from the weights of a population of networks. These higher-level representations are intended to capture information about the models whose weights they describe.

The method applies self-supervised learning to this weight domain using specially designed data augmentations and an adapted attention architecture. The resulting hyper-representations provide a learned way to organize information in network parameters. This addresses the difficulty of understanding weight space directly by asking whether useful model characteristics can be recovered from a representation learned there.

The empirical evaluation shows recovery of diverse network characteristics. The learned representations outperform prior work when predicting hyperparameters, test accuracy, and the generalization gap, and they also transfer to out-of-distribution settings. These results support the idea that weight-based self-supervision captures information relevant to model behavior and training choices. The demonstrated contribution is a useful predictive representation of networks, grounded in the evaluated characteristic-prediction and transfer tasks.
neurips-2021-self-supervised-representat.tldr: Self-supervised learning on neural-network weights produces representations that predict model characteristics and transfer beyond the evaluated training distribution.

paragraphs: Single-image super-resolution reconstructs a higher-resolution image from one lower-resolution input. Standard mean-squared-error and ℓ1 losses weight pixels equally, even though edges and textures carry important visual information and can be difficult to reconstruct. This paper proposes spatially adaptive weighting based on estimated uncertainty.

The network learns both the target image values and a variance estimate for each pixel. Those variances characterize uncertainty and guide a weighted training loss toward challenging image regions. The uncertainty estimates also provide a way to incorporate a sparsity prior when regularizing the reconstruction. The method thus couples learning what each pixel should be with learning how uncertain its reconstruction is.

Experiments on three commonly used super-resolution networks report better PSNR than training with conventional losses. The improvement requires no additional computation during testing, because the reported benefit comes from the training loss. These results support uncertainty estimation as a practical mechanism for allocating training emphasis across an image, with gains demonstrated across the evaluated architectures rather than confined to one network design.
neurips-2021-uncertainty-driven-loss-for.tldr: A pixel-wise uncertainty-based training loss improves reported super-resolution PSNR across three networks without increasing test-time computation.

paragraphs: Language-model pretraining and a later classification task can look very different, making their connection difficult to explain theoretically. This paper links them through a hidden-variable model of text. In its framework, solving the downstream task requires recovering a function of the posterior distribution over those hidden variables.

The authors analyze both learning a classification head on a frozen pretrained model and prompt tuning. Their text-generating models are hidden Markov models, either alone or augmented with a latent memory component to represent longer-term dependencies. Under specified non-degeneracy conditions, simple classification heads can solve the downstream task. Prompt tuning obtains guarantees under weaker conditions.

The memory-augmented model also yields stronger recovery guarantees than the ordinary hidden Markov model, because its long-term memory makes task-relevant information easier to recover. Experiments on synthetic data generated from hidden Markov models support these theoretical findings. The paper consequently offers a conditional explanation of transfer from pretraining: success depends on recoverable hidden information and the adaptation method's ability to access it within the analyzed generative setting.
neurips-2021-why-do-pretrained-language-.tldr: An HMM-based theory connects pretraining to downstream classification and gives prompt tuning guarantees under weaker conditions than head tuning.
